title_en: A Startup Tied to Donald Trump Jr. Could Get a Historic $15 Billion Loan From the Pentagon
excerpt_en: The post A Startup Tied to Donald Trump Jr. Could Get a Historic $15 Billion Loan From the Pentagon appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Donald Trump Jr. during the Bitcoin 2025 Expo in Las Vegas Roger Kisby/Redux In what would rank among the largest government loans in U.S. history, the Pentagon is considering extending $15 billion to a California-based startup with financial ties to Donald Trump Jr., according to interviews and records reviewed by ProPublica.
The award would be one of the biggest the federal government has given to a firm connected to the Trump family and would go to a defense contractor with a largely untested track record.

The startup, Hadrian Automation, has attracted over a billion dollars in private investment in recent months on the promise that it can build factories that use AI and robots to more efficiently produce precision components for defense, aerospace and other industries.

If approved, the loan would be almost twice the value of the entire company, based on estimates from a round of financing this summer. Hadrian announced that round of investment included “major participation by 1789 Capital,” the venture capital firm that Trump Jr. joined as a partner after his father was elected in November 2024. 1789 also invested in the company in 2025.
A spokesperson for 1789 Capital said it holds a “minority stake” in Hadrian, but the total size of its share has not been disclosed.
Do You Have Information We Should Know About Donald Trump Jr.? We’re still reporting. If you know anything about Trump Jr. or his businesses, please get in touch with our reporting team.
Contact me, by email or securely on Signal, with tips about the federal government and Trump’s businesses.
Contact Me The potential loan is 10 times the size of the largest deal the Pentagon has made in a recent lending spree.

According to Pentagon documents, a loan to Hadrian would be used to build a dozen “automated factories” in a partnership with other defense companies and potentially commercial ones to expand production of munitions, drones and other equipment.

The U.S. military has been dealing with a severe shortage of some types of munitions because of the wars in Ukraine and Iran, though it’s unclear if the factories are an attempt to address those particular shortages.

The size and structure of the deal would form an interdependence between the company and the federal government that could run afoul of long-standing guidance on how to protect taxpayer money, former Defense Department officials said. The government would use taxpayer money to vastly expand a fledgling defense contractor, which it would then presumably award contracts to, essentially paying the company money that it could use to repay the loan.
Pentagon staff have also raised several concerns about Hadrian, including its ability to expand and hire fast enough, the documents show.

The loan is under consideration weeks before Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress. The party’s leaders have vowed to use their new oversight powers to scrutinize the raft of contracts and other actions by the Trump administration that have financially benefited the Trump family and others who work in the administration or have ties to it.

Since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term, firms in which his elder sons hold stakes have won billions of dollars in federal backing. ProPublica recently reported on the Trump administration awarding nearly $40 million to one company to screen for Ebola and other infectious diseases. We also revealed how a White House aide intervened to secure a Pentagon loan of $620 million to Vulcan Elements, a rare earth magnet startup, a few months after 1789 Capital invested in it.

Omeed Malik, founder of 1789 Capital, center, signs the guest book on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange in 2025 as Donald Trump Jr. looks on. Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images Responding to a question about whether the White House, Trump Jr. or 1789 lobbied for the loan, the Pentagon said in a statement that no company receives preferential treatment. “Outside affiliations, investors, or political connections play absolutely no role in the Department’s funding decisions.”

A Pentagon spokesperson also cast the loan discussions with Hadrian as being in “early stages” and disputed that the potential deal was for $15 billion. The spokesperson characterized the size of the Hadrian loan that is under discussion as not extraordinary, saying multibillion-dollar deals with other companies had been agreed to but not yet announced.

In a statement, 1789 Capital said it does not get involved in government contracts sought by the companies it invests in but is excited about Hadrian. “Our thesis is to invest in American companies that are rebuilding domestic industrial capacity and reducing dependence on China for critical supply chains that underpin our economy. Hadrian embodies the opportunity we see to strengthen America’s productive capabilities while pursuing compelling returns for our investors.”

Trump Jr.’s lawyer, Alan Garten, said his client played no role in Hadrian being considered for any contract and has no involvement with the company’s operations. “Don is a private citizen who has been building businesses and investing in companies since long before his father first ran for public office. He holds no government position and has never sought to influence government policies, regulations or decisions to advance or benefit his personal business interests,” his lawyer said.
Hadrian did not respond to requests for comment.

In the past, Trump Jr. and Eric Trump have described themselves as passive investors who aren’t involved in federal award decisions and said it is not a conflict for companies they hold an interest in to win government contracts.

title_en: ‘They don’t believe in freedom’: Yemenis plan their escape as Houthis advance on Aden
excerpt_en: With Iran’s proxy fighters encircling the temporary capital, residents and NGOs prepare to evacuate
body_en: Hussein fled his home six years ago after it fell under Houthi control, moving as far south as he could to the port city of Aden, where there was a measure of safety.
The Saudi-backed Yemeni government had made the city its temporary capital; the hundreds of kilometres between it and the Houthis were well fortified.

Today, Hussein is once again considering the painful decision of leaving home. In September, the Iran-aligned Houthis swept aside Yemeni government forces, and now have set their sights on Aden. Houthi fighters are amassing to the north and east of the city, and have begun encircling the government-controlled territory.

“I fled my home in Sana’a and came here. I don’t think the Houthis plan to take over Aden right now, but if they get closer, I will have no choice but to flee again to Marib or Hadhramaut,” said Hussein, who was speaking under a pseudonym.

Hussein works as a schoolteacher and was formerly a member of the Islah party, an Islamist political party aligned with Saudi Arabia that is in opposition to the Houthi movement. He fears that if the Houthis take control of Aden he could face persecution for his former affiliation.
“The Houthis don’t believe in freedom, they just want to hear one voice, the one they like,” he said.

Hussein is one of many residents and organisations nervously watching the Houthi advance. The militia is still about 50 miles (80km) north of Aden, but local people fear government forces may not be able to resist another Houthi assault, having seen the dramatic collapse of government forces and allied militias in September.

Aden has been the seat of the Saudi-backed government of Yemen since 2015. If the Houthis took the city, it would be a huge blow for the government, and a massive failure for the Saudi-led coalition which has for years fought against the Houthis.
The 12-year-long civil war would tilt dramatically in the Houthis’ favour and be a boon for Iran, which has long invested military and political support in the insurgent movement.

Interactive The Yemeni government has pulled back many of its fighters to help defend Aden and the surrounding areas, announcing last week that fighters were redeployed from areas along the south-western coast towards the port city.

Saudi Arabia has tried to halt the Houthi advance with a renewed bombing campaign, carrying out hundreds of airstrikes in Yemen since September, killing and wounding 822 civilians, including 181 children, according to statistics from the independent Yemen Data Project.
Houthi authorities have alleged that Saudi Arabia has carried out 5,500 air and missile attacks since July.

The Houthis have not announced any intention to take Aden, but have instead been amassing troops north of Kirish, and in al-Bayda, areas which, if taken, would cut off the northern and eastern roads to Aden.
“The buildups in al-Bayda could threaten Aden’s eastern road links through Abyan and Saudi supply lines into the city,” said Mohammed al-Basha, the founder of the US-based risk advisory Basha Report.

“The Houthis appear to be testing how well Aden’s defences will hold. If they collapse, the Houthis could try to seize the city. If government forces hold, the Houthis could try to lay siege to it,” al-Basha added.

Houthi forces have begun striking Aden and its surrounding areas, rupturing the relative safety the city has offered for years. Residents have watched anxiously as explosions grow nearer, and displaced people from surrounding areas have started to arrive in greater numbers.
“Since last week, we’ve started following the news every hour. When I get busy, I tell my daughter to follow it and update me,” said Rami, a resident of Aden who spoke under a pseudonym.

The 53-year-old bitterly recalled his experience during the four-month battle for Aden in 2015, when he was stuck in the crossfire between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces. He, like other people in Aden, is trying to make his own calculation of when, or if, the Houthis will arrive.
International organisations are also making contingency plans in case of a Houthi takeover of the city.

“We were informed by management that they are issuing termination notices to all staff this week. If the Houthis don’t reach Aden, they will continue operations and renew our contracts; otherwise this is the end of the road,” an aid worker with an international NGO said.
Already, several NGOs were forced to shut down in the city of Taiz after sweeping Houthi gains.

Not all NGOs would leave in the case of a Houthi takeover, but some are unable to work in Houthi-controlled areas either due to fears for the safety of aid workers, or because the US Treasury designated the Houthis a foreign terrorist organisation in 2025.

title_en: Australia’s inflation rate jumping to 4.9% a ‘very serious moment’ for economy, Chalmers declares
excerpt_en: Figure up from 4.3% annual rate in September and nearly double Reserve Bank’s official target of 2.5%
body_en: Jim Chalmers has declared “a very serious moment for our economy”, after inflation surged to 4.9% in the year to October, from 4.3%, amid fears Australia could tip into recession next year.

As cost-of-living pressures peak in the lead-up to Christmas and unemployment reaches five-year highs, the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Wednesday said the “temporary shocks” of surging fuel costs and the end of electricity rebates drove the larger-than-expected lift in consumer prices.
Related: A recession would probably finish the Albanese government. Here’s how Jim Chalmers is trying to avoid one
The treasurer has been preparing to present a mid-year budget update in three weeks’ time, and he again pledged to deliver “substantial savings” that would help ease inflationary pressures.
Chalmers said 2026 “has been an especially difficult year for people”, but also recognised the limits to how much help his government could give to struggling households.

“There’s no amount of responsible cost of living relief or budget savings, which will make this inflation challenge go away overnight,” he said after the latest consumer price report was released on Wednesday.
Interactive Stephen Smith, a partner at Deloitte Access Economics, said the inflation numbers “underscore the difficult balance facing the federal government”.
“The treasurer must attempt to hand down a budget update that cuts enough to take some pressure off inflation, but avoids cruelling an economy on the cusp of a downturn,” Smith said.

The latest ABS figures showed fuel costs climbed by 6.3% in October, to be about 33% higher over the year. Electricity prices were 25% higher than a year before, reflecting the end of government power bill subsidies.
Rachael McCririck, the ABS head of price statistics, said removing the impact of these “temporary shocks” on fuel and electricity provided a better idea of underlying price pressures in the economy.

But even here, the news was worse than expected. The Reserve Bank’s preferred trimmed mean measure of inflation – which takes out the most volatile prices – lifted to 3.8%. Economists had expected it to stay at 3.6%.
Building costs inflation accelerated to 5.1% in the year to October, from 4.7%, as project home builders passed on higher labour and material prices on to their customers.
Childcare, hairdressing and insurance prices all climbed by more than 5% through the year.
Despite evidence of the ongoing inflationary threat, analysts said the RBA would not be tempted to deliver a sixth interest rate hike at its next board meeting on 7-8 December.
Economists remained confident that price pressures have peaked, and would ease through 2027 as the shocks of this year ebb away.
Brendan Rynne, the chief economist at KPMG, said “today’s inflation jump is not the kind of spike the RBA will be wanting to see, but it’s still unlikely to result in a further rate rise this year”.
“Instead, we expect they’ll hold until February to see how the numbers look between now and then.”
Taylor Nugent, a senior economist at NAB, said: “Our view remains that the RBA is done hiking.”
Nugent said he still expected two rate cuts next year, starting in August, and potentially as many as three in 2027 if the labour market deteriorates more quickly.

title_en: Justice is elusive for the Rohingya even after the ICJ’s landmark genocide ruling against Myanmar
excerpt_en: The prospect of a safe and dignified repatriation of the Rohingya to Myanmar is a near impossibility despite the IJC ruling.
body_en: By nine votes to six, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people in connection with its 2017 “clearance operations” in Rakhine State. The ruling is an alarm bell for all states accused of genocide.

The year 2017 was not the first Rohingya exodus from Myanmar: in 1978 and again in 1991-92, hundreds of thousands of Rohingya poured into Bangladesh to escape state persecution. Many returned, and were forced to flee again when new violence erupted.

Today, more than 1.2 million Rohingya are in refugee camps in Bangladesh without any concrete prospect to return to Myanmar. Most Rohingya want to return, but not without conditions that would ensure their safety. The most crucial condition is the guarantee of citizenship rights.

Since Myanmar stripped the Rohingya of their citizenship in 1982, they have been living under apartheid-like conditions. Among many discriminatory policies imposed on Rohingya life, the Rohingya faced restrictions on movement, education and health care while families were restricted to a two-child limit. Returning to Myanmar just to face the same conditions of life is not an option for many Rohingya.
The repatriation conundrum It’s unlikely, however, that Myanmar will agree to grant citizenship to the Rohingya.
Since the 2021 coup d'état that ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi and her National League for Democracy, the military has had sole control of the government.

Gen. Min Aung Hlaing is seen at the IX Moscow conference on international security in Moscow in June 2021. (AP Photo/Alexander Zemlianichenko) Earlier this year, Min Aung Hlaing, the architect of the Rohingya genocide who had been commander-in-chief of the Myanmar Forces since 2011, stepped down from his role and was subsequently elected president by a military-dominated parliament. This makes the prospect of a safe and dignified repatriation of the Rohingya to Myanmar a near impossibility.

The Myanmar military and government aren’t the only entities complicating the return of the Rohingya. Since late 2023, vast swaths of Rakhine state, where most Rohingya resided until 2017, have been under control of the Arakan army.

The army is the largest and most powerful non-state armed group in the country and it is vying for the independence of the Arakan region, where Rakhine is located. The Arakan army is openly hostile to the Rohingya, and those residing in the territory it controls are facing many of the same restrictions that were previously imposed by the state.
The enforcement deficit The ICJ established Myanmar’s responsibility for the genocide, and consequently ordered it to provide reparations and compensation, with details still to be decided.

But, in practice, there is little the court can do to compel Myanmar to take accountability and pursue justice if it refuses to do so. The ICJ has no independent enforcement mechanism; it only relies on states’ willingness to obey international law.
Only the United Nations Security Council could decide to take coercive action against Myanmar, but China and Russia, which both hold veto power, are likely to oppose it.

The two states have provided Min Aung Hlaing’s regime with political, diplomatic and military support over the years. Each also has its own issues with international human rights law, namely Russia’s war in Ukraine and China’s treatment of the Uyghurs.

How the ruling might help the Rohingya The ICJ ruling has brought much-needed attention to the plight of the Rohingya. Renewed interest in the Rohingya crisis is expected to draw donations that could help alleviate some of the more pressing needs.

Funding for the refugee camps has dwindled in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic and the dismantlement of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID). Currently, the Rohingya in Bangladesh only receive US$7-$12 per person per month in food assistance.
Read more: Thousands are feared dead in Myanmar’s quake. Trump’s USAID cuts will cause even more unnecessary deaths
Combined with the lack of income-generating opportunities, the cuts to food rations are frequently identified by refugees as the most severe challenge they face in the camps.

More attention could also result in stronger political pressure, not just on Myanmar but also on its regional partners. Malaysia, for example, began deporting refugees back to Myanmar in September 2026.

Since the government continues to deny access to international agencies for the refugees, including the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, it could not be verified whether these returns were voluntary, as Malaysia claimed.

It’s unlikely the Rohingya, who make up the majority of Myanmar refugees in Malaysia, are returning of their own free will. International pressure could force Malaysia to stop the deportations and avoid causing further harm to its already vulnerable Rohingya refugee community.

Not ‘illegal immigrants’ Finally, the most immediate benefit of the ruling is that, for the first time, there is a formal recognition of the Rohingya as a distinct people. The ruling directly contradicts Myanmar’s assertions that the Rohingya are “illegal immigrants from Bangladesh” who have no legitimate claim to rights and land in Rakhine.

The ICJ ruling clearly affirms that the atrocities the Rohingya have suffered are indeed genocide, and while it doesn’t guarantee justice for the Rohingya, it’s a necessary precondition that opens the path to restorative justice.

title_en: Mother tongue language rights don’t implement themselves: Lessons from Nepal’s classrooms
excerpt_en: The country has 124 mother tongues and a constitutional promise to teach children in them. But without funding, trained teachers and local-language textbooks, that promise is hard to keep.
body_en: In a Grade 2 classroom in Rautahat, in Nepal’s southern plains, teacher Renuka Dahal holds up a picture card of a mango. She gives the Nepali word, then asks her students what they call it at home. They respond in Tharu and Maithili, the languages many of them speak with their families.
“I ask my students to teach me words in their language,” she told UNICEF in 2025. “It makes them feel that I care about who they are.” And that small exchange marks a real change.

For Canadians interested in Indigenous language revitalization, and for teachers welcoming newcomer students, Nepal’s experience shows what it takes to move language rights off paper and into the classroom.

For generations, many children in Nepal started school in a language they didn’t understand. Yet research shows that beginning school in a familiar language can strengthen learning and make it easier to acquire additional languages, including Nepali and English.
Nepal has written that lesson into its 2015 Constitution, which guarantees communities the right to education in their mother tongue.
A country of 124 mother tongues Nepal is one of the most linguistically diverse countries in the world, though the state has not always acknowledged it. The 2021 census recorded 124 mother tongues.

Fifty years earlier, in 1971, when the Panchayat regime was promoting Nepali above all other languages, the census counted just 17 languages. Today, Nepali is the first language of just under 45 per cent of the population.

I have worked in Nepal since 1991, first as a volunteer schoolteacher and later as a linguist and anthropologist. I have spent decades researching the country’s linguistic diversity. The census numbers reflect a shift I have witnessed on the ground, in communities.

In 2021, for the first time, the census asked people about their ancestral language as well as their mother tongue. Nearly three million more people name Nepali as their mother tongue than they name it as their ancestral language, a sign that many families have shifted to Nepali.
For other languages, the gap goes the other way. Some 300,000 more people name Nepal Bhasa, the language of the Newar community, as their ancestral language than name it as their mother tongue.

Nepali is also spreading as a second language: 46 per cent of the population now speaks it that way, up from 33 per cent in 2011. Whatever pressures Nepal’s other languages face, Nepali is certainly not a language at risk.
Rights on paper On paper, Nepal’s laws side with children. The government’s School Education Sector Plan 2022-32 commits to scaling up early-grade teaching in children’s mother tongues.

In practice, implementation has been sluggish and uneven. As comparative education scholar Uma Pradhan has shown, policy has long treated mother tongues as a bridge to Nepali, a stepping stone to be left behind, with the state offering little support.

In a 2026 study from Tanahun, one grandparent spoke about a granddaughter in Grade 2 who was being taught only in Nepali and English: “She [does not have the] opportunity to study in [her ancestral] language; so, there is a gap.”

Grade 1 students at Shree Sahara Bal Primary School in Pokhara, Nepal, in June 2013. (Photo by Jim Holmes for AusAID), CC BY The evidence for local languages A 2024 study commissioned by UNICEF Nepal examined language use in 30 schools across all seven provinces. Its conclusion was unequivocal. When children learn in their mother tongue or a familiar language, they take a more active part in lessons and do better in assessments and exams.

Many schools have rushed to switch to English-language teaching, often for financial reasons and with little teacher training. Yet students taught in Nepali outscored their English-taught peers in Nepali, in science and even in English, according to the study’s analysis of school assessment results, which was limited in scale.

In Dailekh, in western Nepal, principal Sher Bahadur Rana told UNICEF that teachers once corrected children who used their own “language or dialect.” After training in multilingual teaching, he said, “we learned that children learn faster and feel more confident when we teach them in the language they speak and understand best.”

Obstacles to implementation A recent review by education researchers Pariksha Onta and Amado Padilla, covering 111 studies and policy documents, points to a “persistent disconnect between constitutional commitments, classroom practice and targeted funding.”

Where mother tongues are taught at all, they are usually a subject rather than the language children learn in. Textbooks in children’s mother tongues remain scarce, and most of those that do exist are translations of Nepali materials with little locally relevant content. Far too few teachers who speak local languages are recruited or trained.

Parents, meanwhile, are caught in the middle. Many see English-language schools as a marker of quality and employability. And funding is lacking: in 2026–27, education and sports together received around 10.3 per cent of Nepal’s national budget, well below the international benchmark of allocating at least 15 per cent to education.

Onta and Padilla’s review also highlights what works. In some Kathmandu Valley schools, children learn in Nepal Bhasa for their first three grades before Nepali and English are phased in. A strong foundation in the mother tongue supports learning in the other languages, which means families don’t have to choose between them.
From paper to practice As I argued previously with colleagues Lava Deo Awasthi and Yogendra Prasad Yadava, rights “do not implement themselves.”

title_en: Why are people captivated by this photo of Chris Bowen scowling? Is it the negative space?
excerpt_en: Australia’s climate change minister was president of negotiations at Cop31 in Turkey when it all went a bit sideways
body_en: Blake, I was at the back of the huge plenary hall in Antalya on Sunday at the end of the UN climate summit that overran by two days. For about 20 minutes, you could see from the panic on the stage that it wasn’t going well.

I only had an old iPhone, was a long way back, and remember thinking: “I’d love a long lens to see the expression on their faces.” Then came this incredible picture of Chris Bowen looking like all his Christmases had come at once and every present was a jumper he hates. Why can’t I stop looking at it?
It’s about the natural geometry and negative space in the frame.
It’s tragedy and resignation. On reflection my Christmas jumper analogy probably wasn’t the best. It’s planet-defining stuff, all of this. Sorry, what? Negative space?
That’s the area above his head with nothing in it. It’s shaped like a V and it’s drawing your eyes down to this amazing expression that I’ve actually seen Bowen make before. He does it occasionally.

Yes and no. Not many other photographers have that frame. If the photographer, Murad Sezer, had been a few metres to one side it would have been really different. But he made choices about where to be and what to focus on. Technically, though, it’s not perfect. The lady on the far left …
She is Australia’s head of international negotiations.
Well, she’s cropped in half. That’s not perfect. And there’s a guy with the top of his head chopped off. This is starting to sound bad.

Not really. Murad wasn’t lucky. He would have been looking at body language and the people behind Bowen and then shooting in bursts. I’ve seen the other frames and there’s only a few that catch that expression. We can forgive the cropping because it perfectly tells the story of the moment and what Bowen must have been thinking. That it’s all gone to shit and can this all be over? Well, yes. But the people above him look as though they’re still trying to work things out, actually. So there’s intrigue. Was everything lost at that point? Maybe. The picture was taken before the plenary had started properly. I remember thinking, this looks as though the Australians know they don’t have consensus.

Bowen was president of negotiations and the little sign in front of him seems perfectly placed for the picture. He had to get more than 190 countries – rich and poor, petrostates, fossil fuel producers and low-lying countries that are being particularly smashed by the climate crisis – to agree not to disagree and to accept a pact.

Those of us in the room only knew for sure they hadn’t reached consensus once the meeting got going and countries started interjecting. It was high drama. Consensus is not quite the same as unanimity but it’s close.

I thought you were explaining this to me? They’re political and department staff from Australia. Negotiators, department experts and there’s a senior media adviser in there – she’s second from the right. All exhausted after two weeks and days of all-night negotiations. With so much on the line, I don’t think I would have fancied being any of them.

There’s another brilliant frame from the same day from Khalil Hamra for Associated Press. Again Bowen is wearing an unfortunate expression but this time he’s being chased by a crowd of people with their microphones out, as though he’s Britney Spears. The frames seem to reflect the sentiment that Cop didn’t deliver for the planet.

Well, like the climate, it did all get a bit “toxic”. But we can’t end this on a bad pun. There’s going to be some serious questions asked about how these meetings are run so we secure better climate agreements and don’t have more pictures of ministers who just got lost in the game. Oops, I did it again.

title_en: Coastal areas in England at risk of erosion to receive £11m in new funding
excerpt_en: Exclusive: Laser-equipped drone surveys and road relocations among schemes to get government support
body_en: Laser-equipped drone surveys, sand dune restoration and moving roads inland are among the projects that will receive government funding to help seaside communities in England adapt to rising seas and coastal erosion accelerated by climate breakdown.
More than £11m will be shared between 12 council-led projects that will test ways to spot coastal change earlier and help communities plan for the effects.

Coastal erosion is the gradual wearing away and retreat of the sea shoreline, which can destabilise cliffs and eventually force homes and infrastructure to be demolished before they collapse, leaving people homeless. While it is a natural process, scientists say the climate crisis is accelerating the retreat of the UK’s shores.
Emma Hardy MP, the minister for water and flooding, said the funding will help communities manage the “heartbreak” of losing homes to erosion.

“Coastal erosion is going to happen and it’s going to happen at a faster rate, because climate change is real and we’re seeing that impact,” she said. “This is about being prepared for that coastal erosion and having those conversations [with affected residents] early.”
The Guardian revealed last month that seaside communities along the east coast of England had lost at least 183 homes to coastal erosion and landslides over the past 16 years.
Related: How citizen science is tracking changes in shorelines around the world
The Environment Agency (EA) estimates that 3,500 properties in England will be at risk from coastal erosion by 2055, increasing to more than 10,000 properties by 2105.

More than 6 miles (10km) of major roads, 107 miles of minor roads and 3.5 miles of railway – many serving small, coastal communities – are also at risk from erosion over the next 80 years, according to the EA.

With devastated villages in East Riding of Yorkshire, Norfolk and Suffolk already receiving specialised funding, Wednesday’s announcement aims to help at-risk councils and residents understand erosion, identify when homes will become unsafe, and prepare to move.

Hardy said better monitoring and earlier planning could help councils support residents before erosion made their homes unsafe, reducing the risk of people being forced to leave at short notice and move to temporary accommodation.

Julie Foley, the EA’s director of flood risk strategy and adaptation, said: “Some of the households – who are literally on the edge of the cliff face – they’re incredibly vulnerable people. They’re often some of the most disadvantaged, most vulnerable people in society. They can be very elderly. They may be disabled.”
She added: “This is investment in communities and engagement and support.”

North Yorkshire council, which includes vulnerable coastlines around Filey, Cayton and Scarborough, will use £970,000 of the fund to launch drone surveys. The drones will use laser pulses to measure distances and generate detailed 3D maps of the coast to spot potential cliff movements earlier.

In Cornwall, which has about 500 homes currently at risk of erosion, dunes protecting the coastline are being washed away due to sea level rise and are not being replenished fast enough. The local authority will receive £2.6m to work on community-led adaptation plans and replace the dunes so that they can provide a “nature-based buffer” against waves that crash on the shore. Plans will be developed with residents in places such as Crackington Haven, Hayle, Perranporth and Portreath.

In Watchet, Somerset, cliff movement has forced the closure of the B3191 road, with about 20 properties at direct or future risk. A £290,000 project will use 3D modelling and public engagement to help residents understand the risks and shape a long-term response.
In Redcar and Cleveland, funding will be used to adapt highways, moving a key road into the village of Staithes inland before it collapses due to erosion.

Other local authorities to receive funding include Dorset, Isle of Wight, Northumberland and South Tyneside council. District councils involved include New Forest, South Hams, Swale borough and Wyre council.

title_en: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologizes to staff: ‘I made some terrible mistakes’
excerpt_en: Huang acknowledges he violated code of conduct by having affairs, but denied Trump was instrumental in his return
body_en: Jensen Huang apologized to staff on Tuesday for the tumult he’s caused at Nvidia. The company’s CEO acknowledged he violated the code of conduct for having extramarital affairs, but pushed back on the reports that Donald Trump was instrumental in his reinstatement as chief executive.
“I made some terrible mistakes,” he said, according to a livestream reviewed by the New York Times. “I was unfaithful to Lori, and I hurt my kids and, of course, I hurt all of you.”

The apology came one day after Huang returned as CEO of Nvidia, and less than two weeks after he was ousted from the role. Following a whiplash series of events, the company’s board of directors reinstated Huang on Monday, despite his admission that he’d had an affair. News reports allege the CEO had romantic relationships with two company employees and a suspected Chinese spy.

During Tuesday’s apology, Huang told staffers he was in therapy and that it was “not acceptable” that he violated the company’s code of conduct. In an impromptu speech to employees on Monday, Huang said he was “terribly sorry for putting all of you through all of this” and that he’s “going to be a better CEO the second time around”.

While Huang apologized for his affairs, he rejected narratives that he was a “tech bro” who was “above the law”, according to the New York Times. He added that it was “completely untrue” that Trump pressured Nvidia’s board to reinstate him. The board changed course, he said, because it “evaluated the entire situation” and “gathered facts”. Huang said Trump assured the board that he was not a national security threat.

The US government has been investigating whether Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company formerly run by Huang’s alleged ex-lover, Alice Huang (no relation), diverted Nvidia semiconductors to China in breach of export controls. US government officials have also raised concerns about Alice Huang’s alleged role as a Chinese asset.

Trump reportedly dialed into Nvidia’s Sunday board meeting to advocate for Huang’s return, according to Semafor. Nvidia’s board publicly said on Monday that it reached its decision to bring back Huang with “input from senior levels of the United States government”.

Huang potentially faces two congressional hearings next week, one before the House Foreign Affairs Committee and one before the Senate Banking committee. Gregory Meeks, a democratic congressman from New York and ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said on Tuesday that despite Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia’s CEO, a hearing should still take place.

“The American people deserve to hear publicly from Mr Huang about how potentially billions of dollars’ worth of our most advanced technology wound up in the hands of our greatest competitor, and what role this administration played,” Meeks said.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to request for comment.

title_en: At a Doomed U.N. Conference, Saudi Arabia and Other Oil States Pushed Hard for an Unproven Climate Fix
excerpt_en: The post At a Doomed U.N. Conference, Saudi Arabia and Other Oil States Pushed Hard for an Unproven Climate Fix appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Activists unsatisfied with the second draft text at COP31 hold a silent protest outside the plenary hall, where delegates meet during the United Nations Climate Change Conference at the Antalya Expo Centre in Turkey on Nov. 20. Yasin Akgul/AFP/Getty Images A United Nations-sponsored negotiation on climate change collapsed Sunday amid bitter standoffs over how to slow the warming of the planet and who will pay for it. During the two-week summit, oil- and gas-producing nations blocked any mention of phasing out those fuels — a step scientists uniformly agree is a prerequisite to addressing global warming.
Instead, petrostates, led by Saudi Arabia, pushed for an aggressive expansion of carbon capture technology as a way to reduce the pollution their fuels cause.

Today, carbon capture facilities operate at a tiny fraction of the scale promised, are riddled with failures and setbacks, and show no signs of being able to overcome those hurdles at the pace that the U.N. suggests would be needed to mitigate global warming, reporting by Drilled and ProPublica has found.

The role of carbon capture was just one cause of discord in Turkey at the 31st annual U.N. climate summit, known as the Conference of the Parties. But it reflects a culmination of decades of effort by fossil fuel companies, and the nations most dependent on them, to slow a transition away from oil, coal and gas in part by pressing for methods like carbon capture, which theoretically allow for the use of their products and cleaning up carbon pollution at the same time.

Over the course of two weeks of negotiations in Antalya, drafts of the summit’s main political accord were stripped of language encouraging such a transition even as specific targets were added to expand carbon capture and storage, or CCS.

One draft released Nov. 16 included language encouraging a transition from fossil fuels alongside a recommendation to scale up carbon capture — where greenhouse gases are caught from industry, or filtered from the air, and injected underground — so that it removes at least 500 million tons of carbon dioxide a year by 2035.

Currently, however, the carbon capture industry buries only a sliver of that amount and has struggled for three decades to meet even the lowest-end projections, leading many climate experts to conclude that it will never be a practical solution to climate change.

“The effort by bad faith petrostate actors to block any agreement at #COP31 on fossil fuel phaseout in favor of (hypothetical future) carbon capture is the best evidence yet that moral hazard FUNDAMENTALLY compromises carbon capture as a climate solution,” wrote Michael Mann, a prominent climate scientist at the University of Pennsylvania, in a Bluesky post Sunday.

As it stands, most CCS is used to squeeze additional oil from aging fields, so critics say setting global goals for it would lead to further subsidy of oil production, rather than limit or reduce the amount of CO2 that reaches the air.

Behind the scenes in Antalya, some 700 carbon capture lobbyists were registered as attending, up from 531 at last year’s summit in Brazil and more than the combined delegations of all 14 Pacific Small Island Developing States, according to an analysis of U.N. participant lists by the Center for International Environmental Law. Forty-five of those representatives were granted entry to closed-door negotiating sessions. The center has not completed a similar analysis of lobbyists for other technologies.

By Thursday, as formal climate talks continued, drafters had entirely stripped out mention of a transition away from fossil fuels while leaving the aggressive carbon capture benchmarks intact. When a final draft was proposed Sunday — two days after negotiations were scheduled to conclude — the CCS targets had been made less specific but remained, described as a nonbinding “gigatonne scale” goal.

The agreement — and its emphasis on CCS — “really had the fossil fuel industry’s fingerprints all over it,” said Romain Ioualalen, the global policy lead for the nonprofit Oil Change International, a research and advocacy group pushing for a phaseout of fossil fuels.
A coalition of nations, including the European Union, rejected the proposal outright.

For years, tensions at the annual climate talks have tended to break down to three camps: Saudi Arabia, Russia and other oil-producing states — at times with tacit U.S. support — which argue for an approach that prioritizes slow changes in the energy system in service of economic stability; the wealthy, industrialized nations, which push for an energy transition but resist measures to pay for both the transition and damages caused by warming; and the low- and middle-income nations, which will sign on to fossil fuel phaseout only if other powerful economies commit to supporting the cost of their transition.

Carbon capture remains just one part of that larger debate, which included other ways to clean up energy sources. But its weight in this year’s talks reflects long-standing efforts to tie climate action to its success, as well as a failure to enact any other meaningful agreement that would slow the rate of CO2 emissions in the first place.

For more than a year, ProPublica and Drilled have investigated the history of carbon capture and storage and the decades-long effort by oil companies to validate it in the scientific community and at the U.N. Our reporting has found that industry funding contributed to influential CCS research at universities, petrostates pressed the U.N. to validate the technology without supporting evidence and climate modelers have assumed it can work at an enormous scale, despite the technology’s troubled real-world track record.

title_en: Delayed Cancer Treatment. Missed Medication. How a Popular Insurance Plan’s Use of Prior Authorization Hurt Patients.
excerpt_en: The post Delayed Cancer Treatment. Missed Medication. How a Popular Insurance Plan’s Use of Prior Authorization Hurt Patients. appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Richie Jones at Stone Mountain Park in Georgia this month. Jones and his doctor repeatedly tried to get his insurer, Ambetter, to cover his cancer treatment. Jones often visits the park for quiet reflection. Matt Odom for ProPublica Felicia tried everything she could think of to get her insurer to cover the only treatment that made a difference in her years-long effort to manage her obesity.

In 2024, after her insurer denied her coverage for medication despite her doctor’s order, the 38-year-old Texan sought the help of consumer advocates. She crafted a detailed appeal. She sent it not just to the head of the Fortune 500 company that oversaw her health insurance plan, but also copied the secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the chair of the Federal Trade Commission.
A short time later, someone called from a number she didn’t recognize. It was Kevin Counihan, CEO of her health plan, Ambetter.

Felicia, who asked to be identified by her middle name due to her fear of reprisals and so that she could share sensitive medical information, calmly told Counihan that she hoped that “something gets done right by me and by my health.”
“I have tried everything in the formulary. I exhausted all options,” she explained on the call, which she recorded and shared with ProPublica.

Kevin Counihan, who was CEO of Ambetter and had once overseen the federal Affordable Care Act marketplace, conceded that a customer’s reported experience with his company had been “a tremendous inconvenience and a real pain in the neck.” Brooks Kraft/Getty Images A veteran health insurance executive who had once overseen the federal Affordable Care Act marketplace, Counihan conceded on the call that Felicia’s reported experience with his company had been “a tremendous inconvenience and a real pain in the neck.” But he assured her that “we really want to get you what you” and your doctor “think is the most appropriate medication for you.”
“I’m working on it as fast as possible,” said Counihan.

Counihan’s call was a rare acknowledgment from the company’s top brass of a pervasive problem. Ambetter, the most popular plan on the ACA marketplace, has one of the worst track records of delaying or denying medical coverage by refusing to cover the costs.

ProPublica has found that Ambetter last year denied these kinds of requests — known as prior authorization — at a higher rate than any other large insurer on the ACA marketplace. Our analysis of Ambetter’s own data, along with interviews with more than two dozen recent customers, sheds new light on the vast and sometimes illogical nature of how the company can block access to care.

Each dot below is a marketplace plan in Texas, sized according to the number of prior authorization requests it reported in 2025. Plans further to the right deny those requests at higher rates. Ambetter plans are shown in red.

In Texas, where Ambetter’s denial rates were above 32%, the company initially refused to pay for a medical scan for a patient with Stage 4 colon cancer because the doctor hadn’t ordered a cheaper, less precise scan first.
In Iowa, where Ambetter’s denial rate was 31%, it approved a patient’s colonoscopy but denied a request for the bowel prep that all patients must drink in advance of the procedure.
In Kansas, where Ambetter’s denial rate was 26%, it stopped covering an anti-inflammatory treatment for a patient with Crohn’s disease because it wanted the patient to try a different drug.
A ProPublica analysis of nearly 200 federal marketplace plans across the country found that Ambetter had the highest denial rates in most states where it provided data.
Ambetter plans had an average denial rate of 25% in states where the company reported data for last year. That’s substantially higher than the 16% average denial rate for all marketplace plans.

Our analysis is based on data that federal regulators required marketplace plans to report and publish for the first time this year. The requirement is intended to offer greater transparency into how often insurers restrict care by denying prior authorization for treatment.

Since the ACA marketplace launched in 2013, there has been little transparency around how often insurers request — and deny — prior authorization. Insurers use prior authorization to limit spending on treatment, equipment and prescriptions. They say it is also intended to ensure that doctors try less expensive and less invasive treatments before pricier ones. Health insurance experts said that the process of how or when prior authorization gets used is largely a black box.

U.S. Rep. Craig Goldman, a Republican from Texas, sponsored a bipartisan bill that would require marketplace plans to disclose more information about their use of prior authorization. “These companies represent these individuals — and yet denying them coverage and not being transparent with what they will be able to cover,” he said. “They’re just not there for the best interest of the people.”
Four former heads of state insurance departments who reviewed ProPublica’s findings said that Ambetter’s high denial rate was such an outlier that current regulators should examine further.

“This is stunning — and not in a good way,” Mila Kofman, a former insurance superintendent in Maine who now oversees the District of Columbia’s ACA marketplace, said of Ambetter’s denial rate. “This is something insurance regulators need to understand. There’s a huge opportunity for regulators to address the improper use of prior authorization.”

title_en: Trump had 4 reasons to ‘convince’ Nvidia to rehire Jensen Huang. Here’s why it matters globally
excerpt_en: Who’s leading Nvidia matters well beyond the US – including the speed at which data centres are built worldwide.
body_en: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang outside the White House with US President Donald Trump and other AI executives in September 2026. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images Just 11 days after resigning as chip maker Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang has been rehired by the company he co-founded, vowing “I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around ”.
The company’s board said its unexpected, unanimous decision came after “input from senior levels of the United States government”.
US President Donald Trump went even further, declaring in an interview that he “convinced them” to bring Huang back. The company had bluntly ruled out Huang’s return just days ago.

But why would a US president meddle so openly in the world’s second-most valuable company? And why does the leader of Nvidia matter beyond the US – including the speed at which data centres are built worldwide?

A trillion-dollar turnaround Nvidia’s stocks plunged after Huang announced his resignation on November 12, following reports of extramarital affairs, one with a woman identified by US intelligence as being in touch with China’s top spy agency and another with an Nvidia employee. Both raised concerns about Huang’s judgement as CEO.
Allegations of previously publicly belittling staff – including a senior executive who temporarily succeeded him as CEO – have also been reported by the Wall Street Journal and New York Times.

Nvidia’s stock closed at US$174 a share on November 11, the day before Huang quit. Within eight days, the share price had fallen to about US$126, knocking as much as US$1.2 trillion off its market value – and dragging down the wider US share market.
On the day of Huang’s return, the company’s shares surged 31% to US$165, pushing its market valuation back up by nearly US$1 trillion.
What’s behind Trump’s ‘extraordinary’ intervention? The relationship between the US government, Nvidia and other tech companies has become really entangled.

Even so, it’s extraordinary for a president to have called one of the world’s most valuable companies and told its board to reinstate the CEO. It’s hard to imagine any president other than Trump doing that.
As an economist, I think in terms of incentives. On Nvidia, I believe Trump had four main incentives to weigh in.
First, there’s the obvious economic impact of Nvidia’s falling share price on the wider US stock market.

Asked if last week’s AI selloff was a factor in his push to reinstate Huang as CEO, Trump said: “Probably so, but the bigger impact was the long term.” Trump added “I made the deal” and that his intervention was “very important” to Huang’s return.

There’s been growing talk in the media in recent months about the “ AI bubble ” bursting. The wobbles in AI stocks became especially noticeable when Nvidia lost about one-third of its market capitalisation after Huang’s resignation.
All of those losses threaten the perception that markets do well under Trump – a claim he’s long made.
While Trump’s intervention in Nvidia is extraordinary by historical standards, it’s not the first time his administration has significantly intervened in the market.
Under Trump, the US government last year took a 10% stake in Intel. It has also bought 10–15% stakes in other tech-related companies, especially miners of critical minerals needed for AI.
The success of AI and tech-related mining companies has become inextricably tied to this administration.

The Financial Times reported the surge in Nvidia’s share price on Monday could have made Trump between US$1.3 million and US$15 million. That’s based on his most recent financial disclosures, which show Trump may have owned as many as 370,000 shares at September 30.
Finally, there’s Trump’s personal relationship with Huang.
It’s been reported he takes Huang’s advice on all things AI to a significant extent, both in private and in public. For instance, Huang recently took a phone call from Trump while on stage.
Huang has been one of the few AI industry leaders who hardly mentions potential downsides of AI. Trump has shunned mentions of AI doomsday scenarios or the need for greater safety.
